readings.title: Visitors at an old workshop
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An historic workshop opened for guided visits. Crowds gathered at its narrow doorway while the rest of the building stayed quiet. The main obstacle was all tours beginning at the same entrance. Groups arrived together after lunch and blocked people using nearby shops. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used arrival counts over several weekends. Guides recorded group size and asked neighbours when the entrance was hardest to pass. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated staggered starts could reduce the queue. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced smaller tours with timed entry. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: heritage visits should respect daily local life. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in visitors at an old workshop, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Explaining a village name
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A tourist sign told a dramatic story about a village name. Local historians pointed out that the tale lacked strong evidence. The main obstacle was a legend presented as certain history. Visitors repeated the story without knowing that several explanations existed. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a review of archive sources and oral accounts. Researchers separated documented facts from stories passed down by residents. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated the uncertainty was itself interesting. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a new panel distinguishing records and tradition. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: honest interpretation can deepen interest. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in explaining a village name, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Protecting a painted wall
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A historic house displayed delicate wall paintings. Visitors leaned close to read a small label, sometimes touching the surface. The main obstacle was information placed too near fragile material. The label made people approach the painting even when they intended to be careful. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used observations of visitor movement. Conservators noted where people stopped and measured whether text was readable from a safe distance. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated better labels could reduce accidental contact. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced large descriptions placed beside the viewing area. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: visitor design can support conservation. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in protecting a painted wall, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A walking route through a town
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A heritage walk linked six old buildings. Visitors often turned down a residential lane that was not on the official route. The main obstacle was a route map without clear landmarks. A short line on the map appeared to include a private path. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a walk with first-time visitors. The team followed new users and recorded where they hesitated or chose the wrong turn. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated one unclear junction caused most errors. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a landmark-based map and one sign at the junction. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: good wayfinding protects visitors and residents. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in a walking route through a town, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
Projects concerning tourism and local heritage often begin with a practical question. People may agree on a general goal while experiencing the same service in different ways. In this case, local organizers invited residents to describe ordinary visits and kept simple records of what happened. They compared those accounts before changing the local heritage visitor programme. The first trial did not answer every question, but it showed which difficulties were repeated and which were temporary. Staff then explained the reasons for a modest adjustment. Clear information helped people understand the decision, including those who would have preferred another option. The group planned to review the arrangement again after more people had used it.

translation.referenceAnswer: 有关旅游与地方文化保护的项目通常从一个实际问题开始。人们可能赞同总体目标，却对同一服务有不同体验。在这个案例中，当地组织者请居民描述日常使用情况，并简单记录发生的事情。他们对照这些叙述后调整了服务。最初的试行无法回答所有问题，但能显示哪些困难反复出现，哪些只是暂时现象。工作人员随后解释了一项适度调整的原因。清楚的信息帮助人们理解决定，包括那些更希望采用其他方案的人。团队计划在更多人使用后再次评估安排。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the heritage visitor team proposing a small improvement to the local heritage visitor programme. Explain the problem, describe a short trial, and say what evidence should guide the final decision.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the local heritage visitor programme. People have noticed all tours beginning at the same entrance, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
